Ferdinand de Saussure. A Swiss linguist whose Course in General Linguistics, published posthumously in nineteen sixteen, established the foundational principles of structural linguistics and semiotics. He reframed language as a self-contained system of signs, a perspective that would dominate twentieth-century linguistics. Saussure distinguished between langue, the underlying system or code of a language, and parole, individual speech acts—a distinction that remains fundamental to modern linguistic thought. He defined the sign as comprising two inseparable parts: the signifier, the sound or form, and the signified, the concept, establishing semiotics as a discipline in its own right. He argued that linguistic values are purely relational—the meaning of a word arises not from its inherent content but from its difference from other words. He emphasised the arbitrary relationship between signifier and signified, noting that there is no inherent reason the word dog sounds like that and means that particular animal. His work was published posthumously by students who compiled it from lecture notes, yet despite this unusual origin, it fundamentally reshaped how linguists conceptualise language as a system rather than merely a collection of words, inaugurating the structuralist school that would define the discipline for generations.
